theme: Great is the LORD in the city of our God
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 48. It is a song of Zion, the city of God. Imagine walking around Jerusalem, counting its towers, and giving thanks for God’s protection.
settingTheScene: Psalm 48 is a song of the sons of Korah and one of the Songs of Zion (see also Psalms 46, 76, 84, 87, 122). Written to celebrate God’s deliverance of Jerusalem, perhaps from a military threat, it praises the city as the place of God’s presence. Following the dedication of the temple, it is a fitting song for the pilgrims who came to worship there.
observation: “Great is the LORD and greatly to be praised in the city of our God! His holy mountain, beautiful in elevation, is the joy of all the earth” (vv. 1-2).
“Mount Zion, in the far north, the city of the great King” (v. 2).
“Within her citadels God has made himself known as a fortress” (v. 3).
“For behold, the kings assembled; they came on together. As soon as they saw it, they were astounded” (vv. 4-5).
“As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the LORD of hosts” (v. 8).
“We have thought on your steadfast love, O God, in the midst of your temple” (v. 9).
“Walk about Zion, go around her, number her towers, consider well her ramparts” (vv. 12-13).
“That you may tell the next generation that this is God, our God forever and ever. He will guide us forever” (vv. 13-14).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a declaration of the greatness of God, and then celebrates the city where he lives. Zion is called beautiful in elevation, the joy of all the earth. It is not praised because of its architecture or defenses, but because of who lives there. “God has made himself known as a fortress” within her. The city’s security is the LORD himself.

The picture of the kings assembling and being astounded is dramatic. They see the city and flee in panic. It does not describe a human victory. They are overcome by the sight of God’s presence. The psalm echoes the stories of Jerusalem’s deliverance, perhaps in the days of Jehoshaphat or Hezekiah.

Verse 9 gives the center: “We have thought on your steadfast love, O God, in the midst of your temple.” The temple is not a source of national pride. It is a place to meditate on the covenant love of God. And that praise reaches “to the ends of the earth.”

The psalm then gives a unique invitation: “Walk about Zion, go around her, number her towers.” Pilgrims are told to go around the city and look carefully, as if to say, “Check for yourself. Count the towers.” The purpose is not tourism. It is so that “you may tell the next generation that this is God, our God forever and ever.” The tour is for the sake of testimony. Remembering what God has done is a duty to the young.

The psalm ends with a promise: “He will guide us forever.” The God who lives in Zion is not just a defender but a guide. The psalm makes the city a symbol of the permanent protection of God’s people.
connection: Hebrews 12:22-24 says that believers have come “to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem,” and to Jesus. Matthew 5:35 calls Jerusalem “the city of the great King.” Revelation 21 describes the New Jerusalem coming down from heaven, safe forever. Jesus said he would build his church, and the gates of hell would not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18).
application:
Walk around your own “Zion” in your mind and count what God has done for your church and family. Tell it to someone younger.

Ask where you are depending on your own towers rather than on God.

Meditate on God’s steadfast love in prayer or in worship this week.
prayerPrompts: Praise God, in your own words, for being great.
Tell him what you have thought on of his steadfast love.
Ask him to help you tell someone younger that this is God.
